title: Mutual funds to pay for your child's education
summary: How mutual funds can build a child's education fund: count the years left, how risk comes down as the date nears, and what SEBI changed for children's funds.
body_markdown:
Mutual funds can build your child's education fund through a monthly SIP. A mutual fund is a pool of money from many people, invested by a professional manager under SEBI's rules. A SIP, or systematic investment plan, puts in a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly.


What decides the kind of fund is how many years are left before the fees fall due, not the child's age. The years left decide how much risk the money can carry. SEBI stopped new children's funds in February 2026 and created life cycle funds, which lower risk towards a target year by rule. Children's funds that already existed can carry on.


## How can mutual funds help pay for your child's education?


Mutual funds let you build the fees in small monthly instalments instead of finding a large sum on the day. The plan rests on three things. They are the year the first fee falls due, how many years that leaves, and how the money's risk comes down as that date nears.


Two words matter here. Equity means shares of companies, and it can fall sharply, as the 2020 example further down shows. Debt means loans to governments, banks or companies, in the form of bonds and similar paper. A fund's mix is how much of its money sits in each.


The[guide to SIPs](https://koshex.com/blog/systematic-investment-plan-sip) covers how they work.


## How many years are left until the fees are due?


For the example child, the first big fee is 13 years away, around 2039. The child is 5 today, with college fees expected from age 18.


If the fees are paid year by year, the last payments are further off than the first. Different parts of the money then have different numbers of years left.


The years left point towards a fund category, which is SEBI's label for what a fund may hold. The guide to[choosing a fund for your goal](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-choose-the-right-mutual-fund-for-investment-goals) pairs time left with categories in full. You can browse every[mutual fund category](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories) on Koshex.


## How does the mix change as the date gets closer?


As the fees get nearer, there is less time to wait out a fall in shares. That is why a glide path, a set schedule for moving from shares towards bonds, shifts money as a date approaches.


Look at the 13 years in our example. At the start, a fall in shares has years to recover. Eight years on, only 5 years are left, and a fall hurts more.


A dated example shows how far shares can drop. The NIFTY 50, an index of 50 large companies, closed at 12,362.30 on 14 January 2020. By 23 March 2020 it closed at 7,610.25, a fall of 38.4%. These are price levels of an index, not a fund, and leave out dividends and costs. They are past dates, not a pattern.


Suppose a fee fell due in April 2020 and the money sat in shares. It would have been 38.4% lower on 23 March 2020 than on 14 January 2020. With 13 years left, that is a bad stretch. With six months left, it is a problem.


SEBI's life cycle funds follow a glide path by rule, and the section below shows it. Two Koshex guides cover making this shift yourself:[how to rebalance your portfolio](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-rebalance-your-mutual-fund-portfolio) and[switching from equity to debt](https://koshex.com/blog/is-it-the-right-time-to-switch-from-equity-to-debt) .


## What happened to children's mutual funds?


SEBI stopped new children's funds from 26 February 2026 and created life cycle funds instead. Fund houses could keep their existing children's fund, and several have. Those that remain still lock each investment in for five years or until your child turns 18, whichever comes first.


A lock-in is a period during which you cannot sell at all. For a children's fund it is the scheme's own rule, so read the scheme document before you invest. One fund house's August 2026 factsheet shows an exit load of 1% if you redeem before the child turns 18. An exit load is a fee some funds charge if you sell within a set time after buying.


Against a normal fund, the lock-in is what marks them out. The scheme document of the one you are considering gives its lock-in and any exit load.


## What are life cycle funds?


A life cycle fund is a mutual fund built around a target year in its name, say 2041. It shifts from shares towards bonds on a schedule SEBI fixes.


Target years run from 5 to 30 years away, in steps of five. SEBI fixes the bands, which are the same for every target year:


Years left to the target year Shares (equity) Bonds (debt)


15 to 30 65% to 95% 5% to 25%


10 to 15 65% to 80% 5% to 25%


5 to 10 50% to 65% 5% to 25%


3 to 5 35% to 50% 25% to 50%


1 to 3 20% to 35% 25% to 65%


Under 1 5% to 20% 25% to 65%


Each row also lets the fund hold up to 10% in other assets such as gold and silver.


In its last year, SEBI allows a life cycle fund to be merged into the nearest-maturity life cycle fund, if its unitholders consent.


The exit load is 3% if you leave in the first year, 2% in the second and 1% in the third. A fund house can run up to six life cycle funds at once.


By the end of September 2026 only a handful had been launched. AMFI's price file showed six, from two fund houses, with target years of 2031, 2036 and 2041. A goal around 2039 falls between the last two, so the nearest target year would not match it exactly.


How a life cycle fund is taxed can change as it moves from shares into bonds. Check the scheme documents, and ask a tax adviser before you sell.


## How much might a monthly SIP grow to?


A monthly SIP of ₹8,000 for 13 years puts in ₹12,48,000. What it grows to depends on returns that no one can fix in advance. The table shows three assumed steady yearly returns, each at or below the 12.80% that AMFI sets as its highest rate for illustrations.


Assumed steady yearly return Value after 13 years Of which growth


8% ₹21,97,919 ₹9,49,919


10% ₹25,64,797 ₹13,16,797


12% ₹30,07,449 ₹17,59,449


These are assumptions for illustration, not a forecast. Real returns vary and can be negative. The figures are before tax, and past performance may or may not be sustained in future.


Try your own numbers in the[SIP calculator](https://koshex.com/calculators/sip-calculator) . If your income rises, raising the instalment each year is one way to invest more over time, and the[step-up SIP guide](https://koshex.com/blog/step-up-sip) shows the arithmetic.


## Does investing for education save tax?


A children's fund carries no tax deduction of its own. ELSS (equity linked savings scheme) is the mutual fund category built for the deduction in section 123 (the old Section 80C). It applies under the old tax regime only. SEBI's category name is "ELSS – Tax Saver Fund".


Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 works like this.


- Under the old tax regime only, it allows a deduction of up to ₹1,50,000 in total across all its listed items. It applies to individuals and Hindu Undivided Families.
- The new regime, the default one, has no such deduction.
- An ELSS fund keeps at least 80% in equity. Each purchase is locked in for three years from the date of allotment, so each SIP instalment has its own three years.
- Certain pension funds set up by a mutual fund, as notified by the Central Government, qualify too.
- Tuition fees also count within the same limit. They are fees paid to a university, college, school or other institution in India, for full-time education of up to two of your children. Development fees and donations do not count.


The tuition-fee deduction is for fees paid, not for any investment.


When you sell, gains are taxed by the fund's type. An equity-oriented fund is one that keeps at least 65% in shares of Indian listed companies. If you sell its units within 12 months, the short-term gain is taxed at 20%. A long-term gain, on units held more than 12 months, is taxed at 12.5% on the part above ₹1,25,000 in the tax year.


A Specified Mutual Fund is one that invests more than 65% in debt and money market instruments. Its units bought on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at your slab rate whatever the holding period. See the[ELSS category page](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/elss-funds) for the fund details.


## Whose name should the investment be in?


You can invest in your own name or in the child's, and each has its own rules. A guardian can invest in a minor's name on Koshex; the guardian uses the app and makes the decisions.


[The guide to investing in a minor's name](https://koshex.com/blog/pros-cons-of-investing-in-mutual-funds-in-a-minors-name) covers how an account in a child's name works and what happens when the child turns 18. It also covers how its gains are taxed.


Mutual funds are one route among several. The[non-mutual-fund options for a child](https://koshex.com/blog/3-best-investment-options-for-your-child-in-india) cover products such as the Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana and the Public Provident Fund.[Fixed deposits for children](https://koshex.com/blog/fixed-deposit-for-children) covers the bank route.


Koshex, an app run by an AMFI-registered mutual fund distributor, helps you choose a fund that suits your goal and timeline. It reviews your holdings over time and flags changes, and helps with the ELSS and section 123 decision each financial year.
